title: 1 Kings 22:41–53
context: The chapter closes with notices of two reigns: Jehoshaphat of Judah, who walked in the way of Asa and did right in the LORD’s eyes though the high places remained, and Ahaziah son of Ahab, who did evil and served Baal. Jehoshaphat makes peace with Israel, removes the remaining sodomites, and his ships to Ophir wreck at Ezion Geber. Both traditions read these notices as shared ground, and the regnal synchronisms and the account of the ships (compare 2 Chr 20:35–37) raise chronology and textual questions discussed by interpreters.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.” Arminian readers note the shift from Ahab’s death to the record of Judah’s king.

The synchronisms between the two kingdoms in this section are discussed by interpreters, and several solutions have been proposed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the narrative return to the line of David, through which God kept his promise (2 Sam 7:16).

Both traditions note that the regnal dates in 22:41, 22:51, 2 Kings 1:17, and 2 Kings 3:1 raise chronology questions left unresolved here.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when he began to reign and reigned twenty-five years; his mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi. Arminian readers note the long and stable reign.

2 Chronicles 20:31 gives the same figures.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness in giving Judah a lasting reign under a king who sought him.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the naming of the queen mother is a regular feature of Judah’s royal records.

verses.text: He walked in all the way of Asa his father. He didn’t turn away from it, doing that which was right in the LORD’s eyes. However, the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat “walked in all the way of Asa his father... doing that which was right in the LORD’s eyes. However, the high places were not taken away.” Arminian readers note the honest assessment: real faithfulness, with gaps.

2 Chronicles 17:6 and 20:33 speak differently about the high places, which interpreters discuss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a godly king whose reforms were genuine but incomplete.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and an encouragement: God commends real faithfulness even where obedience is not yet complete.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.” Arminian readers note that peace between the kingdoms ended a long conflict, a real good.

The Chronicler also shows that the alliance had costs (2 Chr 19:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see both the benefit and the danger of the peace, since it brought Judah close to Ahab’s house (cf. 2 Kgs 8:18).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: making peace is good, but the terms and partners matter.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he fought, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Jehoshaphat’s acts, “and his might that he showed, and how he fought,” are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers note that his strength is remembered.

2 Chronicles 17–20 records more of his reign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s blessing on a king who sought him, including his reforms in 2 Chronicles 17 and 19.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Kings gives a brief summary, and the Chronicler fills in more.

verses.text: The remnant of the sodomites, that remained in the days of his father Asa, he put away out of the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat removed “The remnant of the sodomites, that remained in the days of his father Asa” from the land. Arminian readers note that he continued Asa’s reform (15:12).

The Hebrew term behind WEB’s “sodomites” is usually linked with practices tied to pagan worship (cf. 14:24), though its exact meaning is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a constructive act of reform, completing what his father had begun.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: faithful leaders continue the good work of those before them.

verses.text: There was no king in Edom. A deputy ruled.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There was no king in Edom. A deputy ruled.” Arminian readers note that this explains Judah’s access to the port at Ezion Geber in the next verse.

The arrangement may reflect Judah’s control of Edom at the time, though the text does not say so directly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the brief note as background for the ships in verse 48.

Both traditions note that Edom’s later revolt is recorded in 2 Kings 8:20, and that the political situation here is described only briefly.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they didn’t go, for the ships wrecked at Ezion Geber.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they wrecked at Ezion Geber. Arminian readers note that the venture recalls Solomon’s fleet (9:26–28).

The text gives no reason for the wreck here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that 2 Chronicles 20:35–37 presents the wreck as judgment on an alliance with Ahaziah.

Both traditions treat the relationship between the two accounts as a textual question discussed by interpreters and left unresolved here.

verses.text: Then Ahaziah the son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let my servants go with your servants in the ships.” But Jehoshaphat would not.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahaziah asks to send his servants with Jehoshaphat’s servants in the ships, “But Jehoshaphat would not.” Arminian readers note that Jehoshaphat declines a further partnership with Israel.

His refusal may reflect a lesson learned, though the text does not give his motive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that 2 Chronicles 20:35–37 describes Jehoshaphat joining Ahaziah in the shipbuilding, which seems to differ from this verse.

Both traditions treat the relationship between the two accounts as an open textual question, left unresolved here.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in his father David’s city. Jehoram his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried in David’s city, and Jehoram his son reigned. Arminian readers note the peaceful end of a faithful reign.

The Davidic line continues.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God preserving the line of David through Jehoshaphat’s son (cf. 2 Sam 7:16).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Jehoshaphat’s reign closes with honor, though his son will marry into Ahab’s house (2 Kgs 8:18).

verses.text: Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahaziah son of Ahab began to reign “in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years.” Arminian readers note the brief reign.

The synchronism with 2 Kings 3:1 raises chronology questions, often explained by inclusive counting, though this is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the continuing line of Ahab’s house under judgment.

Both traditions note the chronology question as unresolved and treat the short reign as part of the narrative of Ahab’s house.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and walked in the way of his father, and in the way of his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, in which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahaziah “did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and walked in the way of his father, and in the way of his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.” Arminian readers note that he followed the example he was given.

Each generation chooses, yet influence is real.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see sin passed through families and leadership.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Ahaziah is responsible for his own evil, even though he walked in a path his parents and Jeroboam had set.

verses.text: He served Baal and worshiped him, and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger in all the ways that his father had done so.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He served Baal and worshiped him, and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger.” Arminian readers note that Ahaziah’s reign continues the idolatry of Ahab’s house.

The narrative continues in 2 Kings 1, where he seeks Baal Zebub.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the persistence of idolatry and God’s just anger against it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the book ends with a warning, and the story continues in 2 Kings with God’s patience and judgment.
